content_html:
A certificate of deposit (CD) pays a fixed rate in exchange for leaving your money with the bank for a set term. This calculator shows what a CD will be worth when it matures, how much interest it earns and, if you enter your tax rate, how much of that interest you keep.

How to use this calculator

  1. Initial deposit: the amount you put into the CD when you open it.
  2. Interest rate and rate type: enter the rate exactly as the bank quotes it and say whether it is an APY or an interest rate (APR). Most CD offers in the US are advertised by APY.
  3. Term: the length of the CD in months. A 1-year CD is 12 months and a 5-year CD is 60.
  4. Compounding: how often the bank credits interest. With an APY the maturity value does not depend on this setting; with an APR it does.
  5. More options: your marginal tax rate, to estimate the interest left after income tax.

How CD interest is calculated

The calculator first converts the rate to an annual yield. An APR r compounded n times a year gives APY = (1 + r/n)n − 1; with continuous compounding it is er − 1. The balance after m months is then:

Balance = Deposit × (1 + APY)m/12

When you enter an APY, the calculator also shows the equivalent interest rate for the compounding you chose, which is the figure banks call the interest rate in their disclosures.

A worked example

A $10,000 deposit in a 24-month CD with a 4% APY grows to $10,816.00, earning $816.00. With monthly compounding, that APY corresponds to an interest rate of about 3.928%.

If the same CD were quoted as a 4% interest rate compounded monthly, the APY would be 4.074% and the balance at maturity $10,831.43, earning $831.43. At a 22% marginal tax rate, about $182.91 of that would go to income tax, leaving $648.52. The difference shows why it matters which kind of rate a bank is quoting.

Things to check before you open a CD

  • Compare by APY. APY puts every offer on the same footing regardless of compounding frequency.
  • Early withdrawal penalties. Taking money out before maturity usually costs several months of interest. This calculator assumes you hold the CD to the end of its term.
  • Taxes. CD interest is generally taxed as ordinary income in the year it is credited, even if you leave it in the CD.
  • Deposit insurance. CDs at FDIC-insured banks and NCUA-insured credit unions are covered up to the standard limit per depositor, per institution and ownership category.
  • Laddering. Splitting money across CDs with different maturities keeps some cash coming available regularly while still earning term rates.

faq.question: What is the difference between APY and APR on a CD?
faq.answer: The interest rate (APR) is the annual rate before compounding. The APY includes the effect of compounding over a year, so it is the better number for comparing CDs. A 4% rate compounded monthly equals an APY of about 4.074%.

faq.question: Does compounding frequency matter if I know the APY?
faq.answer: Not for the final balance. The APY already reflects the compounding, so two CDs with the same APY and term end with the same amount. Compounding only changes how the interest is spread across the term.

faq.question: Is CD interest taxable?
faq.answer: Yes, in most cases. Interest from a CD in a regular account is taxed as ordinary income for the year it is credited, and your bank reports it on Form 1099-INT. CDs held inside an IRA follow the rules of the IRA instead.

faq.question: What happens when my CD matures?
faq.answer: Banks usually give a short grace period, often around 7 to 10 days, to withdraw the money or move it. If you do nothing, many CDs renew automatically for the same term at the rate offered at that time.

faq.question: Is my information stored or sent anywhere?
faq.answer: No. The calculation runs entirely in your browser, and nothing you enter is sent to a server or saved.
